18.text: BIRD-HUNTING. — Sea-fowl, such as eider-ducks, guillemots, and puffins,

19.text: are caught with various kinds of snares. These are made of whalebone and

20.text: sinew thread, and some of them (Fig. 53, a) are quite similar to those of the

21.text: American Eskimo.¹ Many snares of this kind are joined together and furnished

22.text: with wooden buoys (Fig. 53, b, c), then tied to a very long rope and thrown

23.text: from the shore into the sea as far as possible. The catch is best during long-

24.text: continued tempests, when the sea-fowl come near the shore. Other snares are

25.text: spread on the land, close to lakes and rivers, on nesting-rocks for auks and

26.text: puffins, around entrances to nests, or in bushes for ptarmigan.

27.text: The snare represented in Fig. 53, d, has two nooses made of whalebone

28.text: and fastened on both sides of a small stick. They are spread by placing a

29.text: portion of each noose into small tubes made of goose-quills. The snare has

30.text: a long line fastened to the middle of the cross-piece, by means of which

32.text: Another kind of snare (Fig. 53, e) is set across the entrance to nests of

33.text: sea-fowl, already mentioned, so that they are caught when passing through.

34.text: A ptarmigan-snare is represented in Fig. 53, f. Its end is tied to a

35.text: branch, while the noose is spread on the ptarmigan-track. It is identical with

36.text: that represented by Nelson,² which he says is used for marmots.

37.text: Sitting birds are killed with stones hurled from a common sling (Fig. 54).

38.text: When on the wing, they are hit with throwing-balls, which have been described

39.text: many times by travellers both in Asia and America. At the present time,
